the active form of E. coli photolyase contains fully reduced FAD and not a radical FAD, both in vivo as well as in vitro.
the active form of E. coli photolyase contains fully reduced flavin in the in vivo state and that enzyme with radical flavin is not active in DNA repair.
(i) the active form of DNA photolyase in vivo and in the purified state is E-FAD2 and not E-FADH and (ii) E-FADH does not repair cyclobutane dimers in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the active form of photolyases and the role of light and electron donors in photorepair.
the identification of the active form of E. coli photolyase and the role of radical FAD in dimer repair.
the mechanism of dimer repair by DNA photolyase.

E-FADH and not E-FADH.2 is the active form of Esch. coli photolyase.
the active form of E. coli DNA photolyases is E-FAD2 and not E-FADH.
the active form of E. coli photolyase in vivo and in the presence of suitable electron donor in vitro contains fully reduced flavin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
E-FADH in vivo is not active in photoreactivation.
E-FADH does not function in dimer repair and that E-FAD is not the form of the protein in vivo.
the active form of DNA photolyase in vivo contains fully reduced FAD, that is, E-FADH.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the active form of E. coli photolyase is fully reduced FAD and not a flavosemiquinone radical.
the active form of E. coli DNA photolyases in vivo is not a flavin semiquinone but a flavin radical and that the in vivo quantum yield of dither repair for this enzyme is 1.
the in vivo active form of photolyases is the fully reduced flavin, and not the flavin radical, and that the radical FAD is a stable form of the enzyme that is generated during purification.
